summary.text: The core–mantle boundary lies 2,891 km below Earth's surface, where the silicate mantle meets the liquid iron–nickel outer core.
Seismologists detect it from a sudden change in wave speeds: P waves slow sharply and S waves vanish, because S waves cannot pass through the liquid below.
The top of the outer core is thought to be 500–1,800 K hotter than the mantle above, and heat variations here may affect the flows that produce Earth's magnetic field.

facts.label: D″ layer
facts.value: About 200 km of lower mantle above it

facts.label: Temperature jump
facts.value: Outer core 500–1,800 K hotter than mantle

items.prompt: Earthquake S waves are recorded travelling through the deep mantle but never through the outer core. Why?

options.label: The outer core is too cold for them
Iron's magnetism soaks them up
They shear material and can't cross liquid
The boundary bends them into space

items.explain: S waves work by shearing material and cannot travel through liquids, and the outer core is liquid.

items.prompt: How does the temperature at the very top of the outer core compare with the mantle just above it?

options.label: A few degrees cooler
Hundreds of kelvin hotter or more
Almost exactly the same
A few degrees hotter

items.explain: The uppermost outer core is thought to be about 500–1,800 K hotter than the overlying mantle, forming a thermal boundary layer.

items.prompt: Why is the lowest slice of the mantle called D″ ("D double-prime")?

options.label: Bullen lettered the layers, then split his D layer in two
It was the fourth layer drilled into
The letters stand for double density
It honours a scientist whose name began with D

items.explain: Keith Bullen labelled layers A to G; in 1949 he split layer D into an upper D′ and a lower D″.

items.prompt: Like Earth's surface, the core–mantle boundary is thought to have high and low spots. What holds that relief up?

options.label: Tidal pull from the Moon
The core's magnetic field
Weight of the oceans overhead
Convection in the mantle above

items.explain: The boundary's topography is thought to be supported by solid-state convection in the overlying mantle.

items.prompt: Why might conditions 2,891 km down matter to a compass needle at the surface?

options.label: The boundary is one giant bar magnet
Its heat may steer the field-making flows
Seismic waves from there swing the needle
Its rock shields us from the Sun's field

items.explain: Variations in the boundary's thermal properties may affect how the outer core's iron-rich fluids flow, and those flows are responsible for Earth's magnetic field.

items.prompt: A P wave crosses from the deep mantle into the outer core. What happens to its speed?

options.label: It drops sharply
It rises sharply
It stays the same
It falls to zero

items.explain: P-wave velocities are much slower in the outer core than in the deep mantle.
